::: callout-note
## Scope

This vignette states which covariance DeCovarT needs from a single-cell
reference, and how to estimate it. The target is the within-type
covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ that enters the likelihood, not a
biologically interpretable gene regulatory network. The default estimator is linear shrinkage. Three sparse-precision
alternatives are derived in
[3.3 Precision networks](03-3-precision-networks.html)
and scored by the same cross-validated criterion. The application to the
Suppinger gastruloid reference (solver settings, outputs, plots) is in
the
[covariance chapter of the reproducibility book](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT_reproducibility/blob/main/docs/03-covariance-estimation.qmd).

Local symbols, defined once here: $\omega_{gg'}$ is an entry of
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$; $d$ is the maximum degree of a graph; $K$ is
the number of cross-validation folds; $\alpha$ is an FDR level;
$\gamma$ is the EBIC parameter; $\circ$ is the elementwise product and
$e^{\boldsymbol{A}}$ an elementwise exponential.
:::

# The target: a covariance, not a graph {#sec-cov-target}

DeCovarT evaluates a Gaussian likelihood whose covariance is a sum of
cell-type covariances. With one single-cell specimen, the identified
object is the within-type cell-to-cell covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, which enters linearly in $p_{ji}$
([one-replicate regime](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-one-replicate)).
With purified population profiles, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ enters
through $\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$
([convolution](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-gaussian-convolution)).
Either way the estimate must live on the linear count scale of the mean
signature
([normalisation](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-norm-linear)),
not on $\log(1+x)$ or on nonparanormal scores.

Two properties make the covariance, not the precision, the natural
object.

- **Marginalisation.** If the cells of type $j$ have covariance
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ over all genes, the covariance of a panel
  $\mathcal{P}$ is the sub-matrix
  $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}$, whatever other genes
  are measured. The precision of the panel is
  $\{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}\}^{-1}$, a Schur
  complement of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$, not the sub-matrix
  $(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}$. Adding or removing
  a gene changes every partial correlation and every conditional
  variance $1/\omega_{gg}$; it leaves each covariance entry unchanged.
  A covariance entry is a property of a gene pair; a graph is a property
  of the panel.
- **The mixture has no sparse precision.** Sums such as
  $\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ or
  $\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ have dense inverses even when
  every $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ is sparse. The likelihood never uses the
  zeros of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$.

Sparsity of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ therefore buys DeCovarT only a
lower variance, through $|E_j|+G$ free parameters instead of
$G(G+1)/2$. Existence for $C_j\le G$ does not require it: any
regulariser provides that. Interpretation of the zeros and the recovery
theory of @sec-cov-regimes matter for a network, not for the
deconvolution. The default plug-in is therefore a **dense shrinkage
covariance** (@sec-cov-shrinkage). Sparse precisions are alternatives,
judged on the same held-out score (@sec-cov-cv). When the proportions
are known, `CSNet` estimates type-level co-expression from the same
convolution ([CSNet](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-csnet))
[@suEstimatingCellTypeSpecificGene2024].

| Estimator | Data it sees | Tuning parameter | Object exported to DeCovarT | Graph |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shrinkage, target D (@sec-cov-shrinkage) | linear counts | $\lambda\in[0,1]$; closed-form $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ as start | dense $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$, variances kept | none |
| Graphical lasso, unpenalised diagonal ([graphical lasso](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-cov-glasso)) | correlation $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ of linear counts | $\lambda$ | $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{R}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}$ | support of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j$ |
| `SILGGM` after the nonparanormal map ([nonparanormal](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-cov-npn)) | nonparanormal scores | FDR level $\alpha$ | linear-scale refit under the zeros of the support | FDR-controlled support |
| `PLNnetwork` ([`PLNnetwork`](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-cov-pln)) | raw UMIs, offset $\log s_c$ | $\lambda$ | linear moments of the latent $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_z,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z)$ ([linear-moment map](03-3-precision-networks.html#eq-pln-linear)) | support of the latent precision |

: Four covariance estimators. Each has one tuning parameter, chosen by the criterion of @sec-cov-cv. {#tbl-cov-estimators}

# Sample-size regimes {#sec-cov-regimes}

Report $C_j$ against $G$ for every type (and time point) before
reading any estimate. In the Suppinger reference several types have
$C_j<G$, so the sample covariance $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ has rank at most
$C_j-1$ and no unpenalised estimator exists for them. Three thresholds
are often conflated.

1. **The penalised estimate exists.** With an off-diagonal penalty, the
   graphical lasso has a unique positive definite solution for any
   $\lambda>0$ once every $V_{gg}>0$, even when $C_j<G$
   [@carterExistencePenalisedLikelihood2025]. Shrinkage towards a
   positive definite target exists for any $C_j\ge2$. No sparsity of
   the truth is needed.
2. **The maximum-likelihood estimate on a fixed graph exists.**
   Dempster's refit under the zeros of a graph $E$,

   $$
   \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{E}
   =\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succ0}
   \log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}-\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{V}_j\boldsymbol{\Omega})
   \quad\text{s.t.}\quad
   \omega_{gg'}=0\ \ \forall\,(g,g')\notin E,
   $$ {#eq-hard-cov-selection}

   exists for almost every sample once $C_j$ reaches the
   maximum-likelihood threshold $\operatorname{mlt}(E)$. That threshold
   lies between the clique number and the treewidth plus one, and
   equals the clique number for chordal graphs (Uhler 2012; Bernstein
   & Outlaw 2023).
   <!-- TODO-cite: Uhler 2012, doi:10.1214/11-AOS957 -->
   <!-- TODO-cite: Bernstein & Outlaw 2023, arXiv:2312.03145 -->
   Bernstein and Outlaw simulate graphs selected by the graphical lasso
   from independent Gaussian data ($G\le9$): the probability that
   $C_j\ge\operatorname{mlt}$ of the selected graph rises with $\lambda$
   and with $C_j$; with a single observation the graphical lasso never
   returned the empty graph, the only graph whose estimate then exists
   (pp. 4–5).
3. **The graph is recovered.** Support recovery by the graphical lasso
   needs $C_j\gtrsim d^{2}\log G$, an irrepresentability condition,
   bounded eigenvalues and a minimum $|\omega_{gg'}|$ (Ravikumar et al.
   2011). <!-- TODO-cite: Ravikumar, Wainwright, Raskutti & Yu 2011, doi:10.1214/11-EJS631 -->
   Neighbourhood selection needs $d\log G$
   [@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 41], under its own
   neighbourhood stability condition (Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2006,
   assumption 6).
   <!-- TODO-cite: Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2006, doi:10.1214/009053606000000281 -->
   With $G=500$ and $d=10$, $d^{2}\log G\approx620$ before constants,
   and hubs raise $d$. On models derived from gene expression the
   irrepresentability conditions never held
   [@heinävaaraInconsistencyℓ1penalisedSparse2016], and they involve
   the unknown $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$: "we can never verify them on
   real data" [@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 77].

The consequence for DeCovarT: threshold 1 is all the plug-in needs.
Threshold 2 governs the refits used by `SILGGM` ([nonparanormal](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-cov-npn)).
Threshold 3 governs any biological reading of the zeros, which is out
of scope here; it can be probed by simulating precisions at the
observed $C_j$ with `simulate_hierarchical_grn_moments()` and measuring
recovery.

# Estimators {#sec-cov-estimators}

## Linear shrinkage (default) {#sec-cov-shrinkage}

Schäfer and Strimmer shrink the sample covariance towards a target
$\boldsymbol{T}$, $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\lambda\boldsymbol{T}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{V}_j$
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, eq. 3]. Their target D
("diagonal, unequal variance") keeps the variances and shrinks the
correlations towards zero (Table 1, eq. 10):

$$
\hat\Sigma_{gg}=V_{gg},
\qquad
\hat\Sigma_{gg'}=(1-\lambda)\,R_{j,gg'}\sqrt{V_{gg}V_{g'g'}},
\qquad
\hat\lambda^{\ast}
=\frac{\sum_{g\neq g'}\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(R_{j,gg'})}
      {\sum_{g\neq g'}R_{j,gg'}^{2}},
$$ {#eq-shrink-target-d}

with $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ truncated to $[0,1]$. The closed form
minimises the Frobenius risk (Ledoit–Wolf lemma; Ledoit & Wolf 2004).
<!-- TODO-cite: Ledoit & Wolf 2004, doi:10.1016/S0047-259X(03)00096-4 -->
The estimate is positive definite for any $C_j$ and $G$, invariant to
the scale of each gene, and costs about two sample covariances. Its
precision is dense; partial correlations and a local-FDR graph can be
read from it if wanted (eqs. 11–15).

The Frobenius risk is not the Gaussian likelihood that DeCovarT
evaluates. $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ is therefore only the starting point of
the cross-validated search of @sec-cov-cv. In `corpcor::cov.shrink()`,
`lambda.var = 0` reproduces target D; the default also shrinks the
variances towards their median.


Sparse precisions are not the default plug-in. The graphical lasso,
the nonparanormal `SILGGM` estimator and `PLNnetwork` are derived in
[3.3 Precision networks](03-3-precision-networks.html). Each still
exports a covariance on the linear scale, and each is scored by the
same held-out criterion as shrinkage (@sec-cov-cv).

# One criterion for all four: cross-validated Gaussian log-score {#sec-cov-cv}

Each estimator of @tbl-cov-estimators has one tuning parameter:
$\lambda$ for shrinkage (searched around $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$), $\lambda$
for the graphical lasso, $\alpha$ for `SILGGM`, $\lambda$ for
`PLNnetwork`. All four are tuned by the same score.

**Score.** Split the $C_j$ cells of type $j$ into $K$ folds. Fit
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})$
on the other folds, exported on the linear scale, and score the
$C_{j,k}$ held-out cells by their mean Gaussian log-density,

$$
\ell^{(k)}
=-\frac12\Bigl[\log\det\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)}
+\operatorname{tr}\bigl\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})^{-1}\boldsymbol{V}_{j,k}\bigr\}
+G\log2\pi\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-heldout-loglik}

with
$\boldsymbol{V}_{j,k}=C_{j,k}^{-1}\sum_{c\in k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})^{\top}$.
The tuning value maximises $K^{-1}\sum_k\ell^{(k)}$ (or the one
standard-error rule). Minus the cross-validated score estimates the
Kullback–Leibler risk of the fitted law up to a constant
[@commengesDynamicalBiostatisticalModels2015, § 2.4.2]. It applies to
maximum-likelihood, penalised and shrinkage fits alike, whereas AIC
and BIC are justified for the maximum-likelihood estimate. The folds
split cells of one specimen. The score therefore measures prediction
of new cells of that specimen, which is the population of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, and says nothing about new specimens
[@zimmermanPracticalSolutionPseudoreplication2021].

**Why a Gaussian score is legitimate for non-Gaussian cells.** For a
test cell with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast}$ and covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$, whatever its law,

$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl\{-\log\phi_G(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\bigr\}
=\tfrac12\bigl\{\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
+\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast})
+G\log2\pi\bigr\}.
$$ {#eq-stein-score}

Only the first two moments enter. The excess over its value at
$(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})$ is, at
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast}$, half of Stein's loss
$\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})-\log\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})-G\ge0$,
which is zero only at $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$.
<!-- chk: V2 -->
The Gaussian log-score is thus a proper scoring rule for the mean and
covariance, which is all that DeCovarT's bulk likelihood uses: the bulk
law is Gaussian by the central limit theorem over many cells, not
because single cells are Gaussian.

**Comparing estimators: nested cross-validation.** Tuning needs one
loop. Comparing the four tuned estimators needs two: an inner loop that
chooses each tuning parameter on the training part of an outer fold,
and an outer loop that scores the tuned estimators on cells the tuning
never saw. Reporting the inner-loop maximum as the estimator's
performance is optimistic, because it is the maximum over a grid.
Compare estimators by their paired outer-fold differences, with the
diagonal covariance $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j$ as the baseline.

**LOOCV is not nested cross-validation.** Leave-one-out is the choice
$K=C_j$ in a single loop. It can serve as the inner or the outer loop of
a nested scheme but is not one, and it costs $C_j$ fits per grid value.

**Fast approximation.** The universal approximate cross-validation
criterion approximates leave-one-out from one fit,

$$
\mathrm{UACV}=\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-uacv}

where $\Psi$ is the mean assessment loss (here minus the log-score),
$\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}$ the Hessian of the estimating function and
$\boldsymbol{U}$ (their $\boldsymbol{K}$) the mean cross-product of the
per-cell assessment and estimating scores; the error is $O_p(C_j^{-2})$ (Commenges et al. 2012,
eqs. 6–7). <!-- TODO-cite: Commenges, Proust-Lima, Samieri & Liquet 2012, arXiv:1206.1753 -->
For a maximum-likelihood fit assessed by its own log-likelihood it is
the Takeuchi information criterion divided by $2C_j$ (p. 7). A smooth
penalty enters $\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}$ and lowers the correction
(p. 8). An $\ell_1$ penalty is not differentiable at zero, so for the
graphical lasso and `PLNnetwork` the formula is applied on the active
set, with the support held fixed; that restriction is our reading, not
the paper's.

**Diagnostics, not selectors.** EBIC
[@foygelExtendedBayesianInformation2010] charges
$\log C_j+4\gamma\log G$ per edge and relies on the
maximum-likelihood degrees of freedom; at small $C_j$ it returns empty
graphs ([screening threshold](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-grn-screening)). StARS [@liuStabilityApproachRegularization2010]
chooses the least regularised graph whose edge instability across
subsamples stays below a threshold. It costs $B\times L$ fits for $B$
subsamples and $L$ penalties, targets the support rather than the
covariance, and tends to select too many edges in Gaussian graphical
models. Thresholded adaptive validation targets the support as well
[@laszkiewiczThresholdedAdaptiveValidation2021]. All three are
reported beside the cross-validated choice, not instead of it.

# The diagonal: conditional variance, not self-regulation {#sec-cov-diagonal}

In a Gaussian graphical model,
$\omega_{gg}=1/\operatorname{Var}(x_g\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{-g})$: the
part of gene $g$'s variance that the other panel genes do not explain.
On counts it mixes transcriptional bursting and auto-regulation,
regulators outside the panel, and Poisson sampling, and
$\boldsymbol{V}_j$ alone cannot separate them; at droplet depths
sampling is the largest share for most genes
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]. By marginalisation
(@sec-cov-target) $\omega_{gg}$ also changes with the panel.

**Penalising the diagonal biases the variances.** With a penalised
diagonal the KKT conditions give $\hat\Sigma_{gg}=V_{gg}+\lambda$
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
On the correlation scale every implied correlation shrinks by about
$1/(1+\lambda)$, in the same direction as Poisson attenuation
([count attenuation](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-grn-attenuation)). The penalty does not move the empty-graph
threshold of [screening threshold](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-grn-screening). DeCovarT's likelihood uses the
variances directly, so this bias enters the deconvolution.

**Self-regulation belongs to directed dynamic models.** CardamomOT
estimates a directed self-interaction $\theta_{ii}$ for each gene and
gives it no specific penalty beyond its common $\ell_1$ term towards a
prior network; a positive auto-activation with a negative basal term is
"the most parsimonious way to produce bistability for an isolated gene"
(Maugé & Ventre 2026, p. 28, citing Ferrell 2002).
<!-- TODO-cite: Maugé & Ventre 2026, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014838 -->
<!-- TODO-cite: Ferrell 2002, doi:10.1016/S0955-0674(02)00314-9 (journal line on p. 1 disagrees with the DOI; verify on Crossref) -->
Such a parameter is linked to a precision only through the stationary
covariance of a linearised model. For
$\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}$
with noise covariance $\boldsymbol{Q}$, the stationary covariance
solves the Lyapunov equation
$\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{Q}=\boldsymbol{0}$.
For two genes with self-loops $-a_1,-a_2$, an edge $1\to2$ of weight
$k$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2)$, writing
$\kappa=(a_1+a_2)^{2}q_2+k^{2}q_1$,

$$
\omega_{11}=\frac{2(a_1+a_2)\{a_1(a_1+a_2)q_2+k^{2}q_1\}}{q_1\,\kappa},
\qquad
\omega_{22}=\frac{2a_2(a_1+a_2)^{2}}{\kappa},
\qquad
\omega_{12}=-\frac{2a_2(a_1+a_2)k}{\kappa}.
$$ {#eq-lyapunov-two-gene}

<!-- chk: V5 -->
Each diagonal entry depends on both self-loops, the edge and both noise
levels; only for $k=0$ does it reduce to $2a_g/q_g$, which still mixes
the self-loop with the noise. For a three-gene chain $1\to2\to3$ the
stationary $\omega_{13}$ is non-zero for generic parameters although
genes 1 and 3 share no edge. <!-- chk: V5 (three-gene chain) -->
A GGM diagonal is therefore neither a self-loop nor its sign. Strong
positive self-loops also produce bistable, hence bimodal, within-type
laws, which a Gaussian $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ cannot represent; the
DeCovarT counterpart is to split the type into subtypes.

::: callout-important
## Decision

Never penalise the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$: `glasso` with
`penalize.diagonal = FALSE`, `PLNnetwork` with an unpenalised diagonal,
shrinkage target D with `lambda.var = 0`. Schemes that re-estimate the
diagonal after the off-diagonal step are compatible with this rule:
SPACE estimates conditional variances from residuals
[@pengPartialCorrelationEstimation2009]; the partial-correlation
graphical lasso penalises only the partial correlations and is scale
invariant, computed by alternating the two blocks
[@carterExistenceOptimisationPartial2025]; the simplest version is a
refit without penalty on a selected support (@eq-hard-cov-selection).
:::



A near-diagonal precision is not, by itself, evidence that genes are
independent. The five competing explanations, the screening threshold
and the count attenuation are in
[3.3 Precision networks](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-grn-diagonal).
Directed Gaussian networks and joint estimation across types are in
the same vignette. Graph scores (Hamming distance, structural Hamming
distance, BEELINE, stability selection used as a graph rule) do not
choose $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$. The plug-in is the
covariance with the best held-out Gaussian log-score (@sec-cov-cv).
Those score definitions stay in the reproducibility file
`docs/05-grn-metrics.qmd`, which is not a listed chapter.
